common_name: Mary Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Mary Rose is a reliably vigorous, bushy English rose that has proven itself over decades as a garden-worthy, disease-tolerant performer.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Bred by David Austin and introduced in 1983 alongside Graham Thomas, Mary Rose carries loosely cupped, informal rosette flowers in a warm rose-pink with a light, sweet, old-rose myrrh fragrance, on a bushy, well-branched shrub that has remained a garden favorite for its dependable repeat bloom and forgiving nature. It tolerates a wider range of conditions than many English roses and continues flowering from late spring through frost with only routine care, making it a good starting point for gardeners new to growing old-fashioned-style roses.

common_name: Lady of Shalott Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Lady of Shalott is known for exceptional disease resistance and vigor even in hot, humid climates, and can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a short climber.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2009, Lady of Shalott bears warm apricot-orange, tea-and-spice-scented blooms that open from red-orange buds into loosely cupped rosettes, held on strong, arching, thorny canes that resist bending in rain far better than many old-style roses. It is one of the most disease-resistant and heat-tolerant English roses available, holding up well to Gulf South humidity and blooming almost continuously from late spring through frost, and its vigorous growth allows it to be trained as a short climber against a fence or trellis if given support.

common_name: Wollerton Old Hall Rose (David Austin English Climbing Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation and support for training, since Wollerton Old Hall is vigorous enough to be grown as a short climber against a wall, fence, or pillar.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing a trellis, pillar, or fence if training the vigorous canes as a climber; prune lightly to shape after the main flush rather than hard-pruning, which sacrifices height. Introduced by David Austin in 2011, Wollerton Old Hall produces soft apricot-cream, cupped rosette flowers carrying one of the strongest myrrh fragrances of any English rose, on long, arching, thornier-than-average canes that can reach 10 feet or more when trained upright, or be kept as a large freestanding shrub with pruning. Its vigor, fragrance, and repeat bloom from late spring through frost have made it a favorite for both border and climbing use in warm-climate gardens.

common_name: Darcey Bussell Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Darcey Bussell's compact, bushy habit fits smaller borders and mixed plantings better than the larger, more sprawling English rose cultivars.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2006 and named for the celebrated British ballerina, Darcey Bussell produces deep crimson-red, fully double rosette flowers with a fruity, slightly musky fragrance on a compact, upright, well-branched shrub noticeably smaller and tidier than many older English rose cultivars. Its manageable size and rich, saturated color make it a strong choice for a smaller border or mixed planting where a full-size climbing English rose would be out of scale, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Kent Beauty Oregano (Ornamental Hop-Flowered Trailing Oregano)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants after the last hard frost in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; Kent Beauty is grown almost entirely for its ornamental flower bracts rather than for culinary use and is best sited where its trailing stems can spill over a wall, rock, or container edge.

directions: Kent Beauty is an ornamental oregano hybrid grown for its unusual dangling flower clusters, in which large, papery, chartreuse-to-rose-pink bracts overlap like tiny hops and gradually flush pink as they age, held above rounded, blue-gray, aromatic leaves on trailing stems. Unlike culinary oregano, it is grown chiefly for this striking flower display rather than for the kitchen, and it performs best trailing from a raised bed, rock garden pocket, or hanging container where the pendant flower clusters can be seen and admired at eye level. Give it lean, very well-drained soil in full sun, since it is prone to rot in humid, poorly drained conditions, and expect it to be shorter-lived than standard oregano, particularly where summer humidity is high.
